content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended the use of rapid diagnostic tests for tuberculosis (TB), particularly in pediatric and extrapulmonary cases. These recommendations also emphasize the importance of adequate staffing and maintaining up-to-date contact details for emergency preparedness. The Health Resources and Services Availability Monitoring System (HeRAMS) can play a pivotal role in updating TB service mapping in countries that adopt this approach. Laboratory services are essential for TB prevention and care, as they provide the foundation for accurate diagnosis and guide treatment decisions. Due to the technical requirements and the need for quality assurance, laboratory services are organized into networks at different levels of care. These networks utilize complementary diagnostic tools and are supported by a robust supply system. The implementation of new diagnostic tests, such as first-line and second-line line-probe assays (FL-LPA and SL-LPA), next-generation sequencing (NGS), and high-complexity reverse hybridization nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for pyrazinamide (PZA) resistance, is critical. These tests are particularly suited for higher-level laboratories and can leverage existing infrastructure. Additionally, culture and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) using solid or liquid media should be available at these levels, with a focus on new and repurposed drugs. The structure of TB diagnostic networks and the testing packages available at each level should be tailored to the needs of the community and the local TB epidemiology. In many countries with moderate to high TB burdens, there remains a significant gap in access to WHO-recommended rapid molecular diagnostic testing for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB). Smear microscopy is still recommended for treatment monitoring in some settings. Novel specimen transport approaches are helping to address these gaps but remain insufficient. Expanding diagnostic resources has been a major focus of domestic and international funding for TB in recent years. The COVID-19 response demonstrated the feasibility and importance of expanding access to diagnostic platforms capable of testing for multiple diseases, which is particularly beneficial for vulnerable populations. TB diagnostic service mapping should also include facilities providing chest radiography, mobile units, and additional diagnostic tools. Treatment services for TB are typically organized into three levels: clinic-based, community-based, and hospital-based care. Clinic-based care involves providing the full course of treatment on an outpatient basis at accessible health facilities. Community-based care allows treatment to be delivered in the patient’s community, such as at their home, workplace, or through mobile health services, with the support of a treatment supporter or community health worker. Hospital-based care is reserved for severely ill patients, including those with drug-resistant TB. Service mapping should account for the location, accessibility, capacity, staffing, and contact details of treatment centers, as this information is critical during emergency responses. In humanitarian settings, such as among Tibetan refugees in India, the introduction of active TB case finding and rapid molecular diagnostics has significantly improved TB detection rates. For example, between 2011 and 2013, a study screened over 27,000 individuals for TB symptoms and tested symptomatic individuals using a comprehensive diagnostic algorithm. This approach enabled the detection of many more cases than expected, including cases of MDR-TB. During emergencies, such as Typhoon Haiyan in the Philippines, ensuring continuity of TB care is a priority. The Department of Health (DoH), in collaboration with WHO and other partners, established systems to trace TB patients and refer them to the nearest treatment centers. Local health staff compiled lists of TB patients from memory when medical records were lost. Treatment centers were mapped and assessed for functionality, and facility maps were distributed to NGOs and foreign medical teams to facilitate appropriate referrals. Within a month, nearly all TB patients in typhoon-affected areas had resumed treatment. Preparedness for TB care during emergencies requires experienced professionals to confirm diagnoses and support treatment. National TB Program (NTP) emergency focal points or qualified personnel from technical partners should be identified in advance for rapid deployment. Expertise in diagnostics, clinical management, infection control, procurement, supply management, and community care is essential. Training on TB preparedness should be incorporated into emergency response planning. Procurement and supply management for TB during emergencies require additional planning to account for potential stock losses and the unique needs of chronic care. Centralized mechanisms for TB drug procurement and distribution, integrated into the general health system, can be leveraged for emergencies if properly planned. Forecasting TB drug requirements should consider population size, available stock, and storage conditions. Emergency grants from organizations like the Stop TB Partnership’s Global Drug Facility can help prevent stockouts during crises. Monitoring systems for TB service delivery must continue uninterrupted during humanitarian operations. Standardized recording and reporting tools should be used to ensure comprehensive monitoring of TB services, including those serving refugees and internally displaced persons. These systems support the analysis of individual cases and overall program performance, enabling the evaluation of treatment outcomes and service delivery metrics. In summary, effective TB prevention, diagnosis, and treatment during emergencies require robust planning, tailored service delivery, and the integration of innovative approaches to ensure continuity of care.
